items.stem: A nurse in a school immunization clinic is teaching parents about human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination for a healthy child with no prior HPV doses. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: Routine HPV vaccination is recommended at ages 11 or 12 years and may be started as early as age 9.
HPV vaccination should be deferred until the child is sexually active so immunity matches exposure timing.
HPV vaccine treats existing HPV infections and genital warts, so it is reserved for adolescents with known infection.
HPV vaccination is recommended only for girls; boys do not benefit from immunization.

rationales.A: Correct. CDC recommends routine HPV vaccination at 11 or 12 years (can start at 9); Merck similarly states routine recommendation at ages 11 or 12 (can start at 9).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Both sources emphasize vaccination before HPV exposure; waiting until sexual activity reduces the preventive benefit.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CDC states HPV vaccination prevents new infections but does not treat existing HPV infection or disease.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CDC catch-up guidance applies to everyone through age 26 if not adequately vaccinated earlier; Merck discusses vaccine protection against HPV types causing warts and cancer without restricting to girls only for the routine age statement.

sources.title: HPV Vaccine Recommendations
sources.publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sources.evidence: Routine vaccination at 11 or 12; can start at age 9; prevents new infections, does not treat existing infection.

sources.title: Warts
sources.evidence: HPV vaccine routinely recommended for children ages 11 or 12 (can start at age 9).

items.stem: A community health nurse is teaching hikers how to reduce Lyme disease risk in an endemic area. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Apply an EPA-registered insect repellent containing an ingredient such as DEET when outdoors.
Check the body, clothing, and gear for ticks during and after outdoor activity.
Remove an attached tick promptly using fine-tipped tweezers close to the skin, pulling upward with steady pressure.
Wait several days after noticing an attached tick before removal so the tick detaches on its own.
Consider clothing treated with permethrin as an additional protective measure.
Assume backyard lawns are always risk-free, so prevention steps are needed only in remote forests.

rationales.A: Correct. CDC lists EPA-registered repellents including DEET; Merck advises DEET-containing repellents on skin in endemic areas.
rationales.B: Correct. CDC advises checking body, clothing, gear, and pets; Merck stresses frequent searches for ticks.
rationales.C: Correct. Both CDC and Merck emphasize prompt removal; Merck details fine-tipped tweezers close to the skin with steady upward pull.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CDC warns delaying removal increases disease risk; Merck instructs removal when a tick is found attached.
rationales.E: Correct. CDC recommends permethrin-treated clothing/gear; Merck notes permethrin on clothing effectively kills ticks.
rationales.F: Incorrect. CDC notes many exposures occur in yards/neighborhoods, not only remote wooded areas.

items.stem: A public health nurse is planning harm-reduction teaching for clients and families at elevated risk of opioid overdose. Which recommendation is most appropriate?

options.text: Carry naloxone and ensure others know where it is, because bystanders can reverse an opioid overdose while awaiting emergency help.
Avoid keeping naloxone at home because using it without a prescription is illegal in all jurisdictions.
Give naloxone only after waiting 30 minutes to confirm the overdose is opioid-related.
Leave the person alone after the first naloxone dose so they can recover privately.

rationales.A: Correct. CDC advises that people at increased overdose risk carry naloxone and that bystanders can give it; OpenStax describes community naloxone distribution and instructs administering naloxone for suspected overdose while calling emergency services.
rationales.B: Incorrect. CDC states naloxone is available over the counter and through community programs; OpenStax supports community distribution as harm reduction.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CDC and OpenStax urge prompt action for suspected overdose; CDC notes naloxone will not harm someone overdosing on non-opioids, so it is best to use it if overdose is suspected.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Both CDC and OpenStax instruct staying with the person until emergency help arrives.

items.stem: A parent calls after a previously well toddler had a brief generalized seizure during a fever. The seizure has stopped, and the child is breathing. Which instruction should the nurse give first for immediate safety during any future febrile seizure?

options.text: Place the child on their side on a flat surface, do not put anything in the mouth, and call emergency services if the seizure lasts longer than a few minutes or the infant is younger than 6 months.
Hold the child firmly upright and insert a spoon between the teeth to protect the tongue.
Give an oral antipyretic during the seizure to stop the convulsions immediately.
Start continuous antiseizure medication at home after a single simple febrile seizure without clinician evaluation.

rationales.A: Correct. CPS Caring for Kids advises side-lying on a flat surface, nothing between the teeth, and calling 911 if the seizure lasts longer than 3 minutes or the baby is younger than 6 months; Merck supports supportive management for brief seizures and urgent medication/support for prolonged seizures.
rationales.B: Incorrect. CPS explicitly says do not put anything between the teeth and do not hold the child down.
rationales.C: Incorrect. During an active seizure, oral medication is unsafe; Merck notes antipyretics may help symptoms but routine use may not prevent recurrence, and management during a brief seizure is supportive.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Merck states EEG/routine antiseizure prophylaxis is not indicated after a typical simple febrile seizure with normal exam; CPS advises medical evaluation after any seizure.

sources.title: Febrile seizures
sources.publisher: Canadian Paediatric Society — Caring for Kids
sources.section: What can I do? / When should I call the doctor?
sources.evidence: Side-lying; nothing between teeth; call 911 if >3 minutes or infant <6 months; see doctor after seizure.

sources.title: Febrile Seizures
sources.section: Treatment of Febrile Seizures / Prevention of Febrile Seizures
sources.evidence: Supportive care if <5 minutes; meds for prolonged seizures; antipyretics symptomatic; EEG not after initial simple febrile seizure with normal exam.

items.stem: An Ontario RN smells alcohol on a colleague’s breath at the start of a shift and observes unsteady gait while the colleague prepares to take a client assignment. Which action best meets professional accountabilities?

options.text: Report the unsafe behaviour to the appropriate persons (such as the employer and, as required, the College of Nurses of Ontario), recognizing nurses must not practise while impaired.
Ignore the observations to protect the colleague’s privacy and avoid a difficult conversation.
Allow the colleague to continue the assignment if clients seem stable, then discuss it privately after the shift ends.
Document opinions about the colleague’s character in the client’s health record instead of notifying leadership.

rationales.A: Correct. CNO Code of Conduct 6.4 requires reporting unsafe behaviour/unethical conduct to relevant individuals including employers and CNO whether or not harm occurred; 6.8 states nurses do not practise when impaired. OpenStax culture of safety/just culture support raising safety concerns and reporting safety events.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Failing to report unsafe behaviour violates CNO 6.4 and undermines a culture of safety.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Allowing impaired practice continues immediate client risk and conflicts with CNO 6.8.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Client records are not the place for colleague character opinions; reporting belongs to appropriate organizational/regulatory channels per CNO 6.4.

sources.title: Code of Conduct
sources.evidence: Report unsafe behaviour/unethical conduct to employers/CNO; nurses do not practise when impaired.

sources.title: 9.1 Safety: Individual and Environmental
sources.evidence: Culture of safety prioritizes reporting concerns and safety events; just culture supports raising questions and reporting in a nonpunitive learning environment.

items.stem: A charge nurse is assigning care for a newly admitted client with complex, unstable needs. Which principle should guide the assignment decision?

options.text: Match the complexity of the client’s care needs to a staff member who has demonstrated proficiency with similar care.
Assign the most complex client to the newest orientee to accelerate learning under pressure.
Give every nurse an equal number of clients regardless of acuity or demonstrated competence.
Delegate nursing judgment about the unstable client’s plan of care to unregulated assistive personnel.

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax leadership guidance on determining clinical ability requires considering care complexity and whether the staff member has demonstrated proficiency in similar tasks. AHRQ notes patient acuity and staff skill mix/expertise as key factors influencing safe nurse staffing/assignment.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Assigning unstable complex care to an inexperienced orientee without demonstrated proficiency violates clinical-ability matching.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Equal headcounts ignore acuity and competency considerations emphasized in clinical-ability determination.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Nursing judgment for an unstable client remains with the nurse; assignment must account for expertise/acuity rather than handing judgment to unregulated assistive personnel.

items.stem: A client receives subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin (lispro/aspart/glulisine) before breakfast. Complete the teaching statement with the most accurate choices.

ngn.template: Rapid-acting insulin typically peaks about {B1} after injection, and the client is at higher risk for {B2} around that peak.

rationales.B1a: Correct. OpenStax and ADA list rapid-acting insulin peak at about 1–2 hours.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. 12–18 hours describes intermediate-acting duration/peak range, not rapid-acting peak.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Long-acting analogs are described as having no peak and ~24-hour duration.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Onset is about 15 minutes; peak is later (about 1–2 hours), not 5–10 minutes.
rationales.B2a: Correct. OpenStax states clients are at higher risk of hypoglycemia symptoms when insulin is peaking.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Peak effect increases hypoglycemia risk, not HHS as the primary peak teaching point.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Vitamin B12 deficiency is not the peak-related adverse effect of rapid-acting insulin.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Opioid withdrawal is unrelated to insulin peak pharmacokinetics.

sources.title: 28.2 Insulin and Non-Insulin Injectable Diabetes Drugs
sources.evidence: Peak = maximum glucose-lowering; higher hypoglycemia risk when peaking; rapid-acting peaks in 1–2 hours.

items.stem: A client develops sudden urticaria, wheezing, and hypotension within minutes after starting a new IV antibiotic. Complete the bowtie: identify the priority condition, two nursing actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Isolated mild contact dermatitis without systemic signs

actions.text: Stop the suspected antibiotic infusion and call for emergency/rapid response help
Encourage the client to ambulate to the gift shop for distraction
Wait 1 hour to see if wheezing resolves before any intervention
Increase the antibiotic infusion rate to finish it faster

parameters.text: Airway patency, breathing effort, and oxygen saturation
Ability to complete a crossword puzzle
Preference for morning versus evening television

rationales.K1: Correct. Sudden multi-system signs after a drug trigger fit anaphylaxis (Merck and OpenStax).
rationales.K2: Incorrect. Isolated mild dermatitis lacks respiratory/cardiovascular involvement described here.
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Constipation does not explain acute wheezing and hypotension.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Chronic stable hypertension does not explain acute urticaria, wheezing, and shock signs.
rationales.A1: Correct. Merck: epinephrine immediately is the cornerstone; OpenStax likewise prioritizes epinephrine.
rationales.A2: Correct. OpenStax directs notifying rapid response/provider and rapid interventions; stopping the culprit infusion is required to halt ongoing exposure while activating help.
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Ambulation delays emergency treatment of a life-threatening reaction.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. Merck warns symptoms may progress rapidly to airway occlusion or shock; waiting is unsafe.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Continuing/increasing the suspected allergen worsens anaphylaxis.
rationales.P1: Correct. Airway/breathing compromise is central in anaphylaxis assessment in both sources.
rationales.P2: Correct. Hypotension/shock risk requires blood pressure and perfusion monitoring; Merck notes IV fluids/vasopressors for persistent hypotension.
rationales.P3: Incorrect. Cognitive puzzles are not priority physiologic parameters in anaphylaxis.
rationales.P4: Incorrect. Television preference is irrelevant to emergency monitoring.
rationales.P5: Incorrect. Cosmetic preferences are not anaphylaxis monitoring parameters.

sources.section: Treatment of Anaphylaxis / Epinephrine / Key Points

items.stem: Emergency personnel bring a client with extensive flame burns and possible smoke exposure. Which assessment and intervention priority is correct during the emergent phase?

options.text: Assess and secure airway patency and support breathing before focusing on other burn wound details.
Complete a full detailed wound tracing of every burn edge before checking the airway.
Defer oxygen and airway evaluation until after a complete social history interview.
Prioritize arranging outpatient follow-up before assessing circulation or breathing.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck states first priorities are ABC (airway, breathing, circulation), with airway/ventilation and smoke inhalation addressed early; OpenStax ABCDE begins with airway patency then breathing, prioritizing airway ahead of circulation issues.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Detailed wound mapping must not precede life-threatening airway assessment.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Social history is not the emergent first priority over airway/oxygenation.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Outpatient planning is irrelevant until ABCs are stabilized.

sources.title: Burns
sources.evidence: First priorities ABC; provide airway, support ventilation, treat smoke inhalation with oxygen.

sources.title: 14.2 Burns
sources.evidence: ABCDE starts with airway patency then breathing; airway prioritized ahead of circulation.

items.stem: A school-age client presents with an acute asthma exacerbation: audible wheezes, cough, and SpO2 90% on room air. For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated at this time.

rows.text: Administer a short-acting inhaled beta-agonist (SABA) bronchodilator as ordered.
Monitor oxygen saturation and provide supplemental oxygen as needed to support oxygenation.
Use a spacer/holding chamber with aerosolized inhaled medication when appropriate to improve airway deposition.
Withhold all bronchodilators until a full set of allergy skin tests is completed tomorrow.
Encourage prolonged outdoor running to 'work through' bronchospasm before any rescue inhaler.

rationales.R1: Indicated. Merck treats acute exacerbations with inhaled bronchodilators; OpenStax identifies SABAs as rescue medications for acute shortness of breath.
rationales.R2: Indicated. OpenStax includes SpO2 monitoring and supplemental oxygen in acute exacerbations; supporting oxygenation is part of exacerbation care.
rationales.R3: Indicated. Merck notes spacers/holding chambers facilitate airway deposition of aerosolized inhaled medications; OpenStax also references spacer use when indicated.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. Delaying bronchodilators for elective allergy testing leaves acute bronchospasm untreated.
rationales.R5: Not indicated. Exercise can trigger bronchospasm; acute exacerbation requires rescue therapy, not forced running.

items.stem: A nurse is planning care for a client with moderate dementia living at home with family. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Maintain a familiar environment with regular low-stress routines and orientation cues such as clocks/calendars.
Ask simple questions in a calm manner and watch for rising anxiety or confusion.
Assess the home for fall hazards such as throw rugs and inadequate lighting.
Frequently rearrange furniture and introduce many new caregivers each day for stimulation.
Encourage familiar family/friends to spend time with the client when appropriate.
Leave knives accessible and the stove enabled if the client has kitchen safety deficits.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck recommends familiar surroundings, orientation reinforcement, and regular low-stress activities; OpenStax supports routines that comfort clients with major NCD.
rationales.B: Correct. OpenStax advises simple calm questions and recognizing increasing anxiety/confusion.
rationales.C: Correct. Merck patient-safety goals include preventing accidents/falls; OpenStax emphasizes environmental safety assessment including throw rugs and lighting.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Merck advises minimizing new stimulation and explaining changes; frequent unfamiliar upheaval is destabilizing.
rationales.E: Correct. OpenStax encourages family/friends spending time with the client.
rationales.F: Incorrect. Merck states protective measures (e.g., hiding knives, disabling the stove) may be required when deficits create danger.

items.stem: A client with mild-to-moderate dementia becomes distressed after being moved to an unfamiliar shared room. Which nursing approach best supports comfort and orientation?

options.text: Provide a bright, familiar setup with consistent routines and clear orientation cues, minimizing unnecessary new stimulation.
Keep the room dark at all times and avoid any clocks so the client is not reminded of time.
Rotate the client through a different unit each shift to increase novelty.
Withhold all personal belongings to reduce clutter regardless of familiarity needs.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck states mild-to-moderate dementia clients usually function best in familiar surroundings with orientation cues, bright cheerful familiar environment, minimal new stimulation, and regular low-stress activities; OpenStax supports comforting familiar activities/routines.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Merck specifically recommends clocks/calendars and a bright environment to reinforce orientation.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Frequent unfamiliar moves increase stimulation and conflict with Merck’s minimize-new-stimulation guidance.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Removing familiar personal items undermines the familiar environment that supports orientation and dignity.
